content: A total of 411 infants were unnecessarily placed on treatment due to false-positive test results. When an indeterminate range was used to identify likely false-positive results, the number of misdiagnoses varied depending on the cycle threshold (Ct) cutoff value used to define the indeterminate range. Lower Ct cutoff values, which deviate more significantly from the standard of care (SoC), resulted in fewer infants being unnecessarily treated. However, this came at the cost of more HIV-infected infants being misdiagnosed. To evaluate the incremental clinical consequences and associated economic outcomes of switching from the current SoC to an indeterminate range policy, we calculated the additional number of infants unnecessarily placed on treatment, missed HIV cases, and HIV-related deaths. The use of an indeterminate range often reduced the number of missed HIV cases compared to the SoC, which is reflected as negative (beneficial) values in the analysis. To illustrate the trade-off between false-negative and false-positive clinical decisions, we analyzed the ratio of unnecessary antiretroviral therapy (ART) averted to excess HIV-related deaths across various scenarios. When priority retesting was implemented for infants most likely to produce false-positive results, the trade-off between unnecessary ART averted and excess deaths became more favorable at every Ct cutoff tested. At a prevalence of 1% (the most favorable scenario tested), adopting a specific Ct cutoff was associated with 318 unnecessary treatments averted per excess death, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 146 to 1,472. Cost-effectiveness analyses showed that policies incorporating an indeterminate range could result in significant savings, estimated at $48,700 (95% CI: $37,700–$65,400) and $379,800 (95% CI: $320,300–$450,800), respectively. Trends in cost-effectiveness mirrored trends in clinical trade-offs. Adverse impacts were compared between simulations following the SoC algorithm, which uses the limit of detection as the cutoff for a positive HIV diagnosis, and variations of the indeterminate range algorithm, where the Ct cutoff was varied from 36 to 30. Unnecessary ART represents the number of false-positive diagnoses of HIV-uninfected infants who receive lifelong ART as a result. Missed HIV cases represent the number of false-negative diagnoses of HIV-infected infants who do not receive presumptive ART. Lower Ct values resulted in more HIV-uninfected infants falling into the indeterminate range, reducing unnecessary ART regimens. However, this also led to more HIV-infected infants being classified in the indeterminate range, increasing missed HIV cases. The ratio of unnecessary ART regimens averted to excess HIV-related deaths was plotted for Ct cutoffs ranging from 36 to 30. A higher ratio indicates a more favorable trade-off, with more unnecessary ART regimens averted for each additional death incurred. Results for the priority retesting variation of the indeterminate range algorithm, where all indeterminate results are retested but no positive results are retested, were also analyzed. The clinical trade-off became more favorable, with a ratio of 320 unnecessary ART regimens averted per excess HIV-related death (95% CI: 144–1,538). The positive predictive value of early infant HIV diagnostic assays decreases as programs for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV are scaled up. In many low-income settings, confirmatory tests are not widely performed, increasing the likelihood of false-positive results. Diagnostic algorithms that define an indeterminate range for HIV results near the limit of detection can reduce incorrect diagnoses of HIV-uninfected children and their associated unnecessary lifelong ART regimens. In low-prevalence settings, such algorithms are highly effective, with a clinical trade-off of 23.8 unnecessary ART regimens averted per excess HIV-related death. When confirmatory testing is unavailable, the use of an indeterminate range can significantly improve the efficiency of pediatric HIV diagnosis and treatment programs with relatively few adverse clinical consequences.
